summary: Postmortem follow-up for the 2025-10-14 partial outage affecting Elysium's inference requests. Root cause discussion focused on combined effects of sudden traffic spike + cache eviction pattern leading to degraded KV cache hit-rate and CPU fallback on a subset of host pools. Action items include runbook updates, targeted bench tests on batching and cache parameters, and proposals for Dedicated/resilience configurations.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-15
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (CSM), Rachel Park (Elysium SRE), Dmitri Ivanov (Elysium CTO), Sophia Lane (VP Eng)

Summary (auto): Follow-up to 10/14 partial outage; agree next steps and owners.

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you making time. We wanted to go through the postmortem, make sure the remediation plan lines up with Elysium's priorities.
[00:15] Rachel Park: Thanks Jordan. Quick note, we got hit around 11:12 UTC on 10/14, increased 5xxs and latency spikes, roughly 23 minutes of degraded performance, most traffic returned after autoscale but residual errors for a subset of requests.
[00:32] Maya Singh: And from our end we saw a cascade where the KV cache evicted hot prefixes because of simultaneous long-seq requests, then fallback to uncached execution increased CPU contention on a small pool. There was also a short spike in cold starts on one host group.
[01:05] Dmitri Ivanov: Can you explain the eviction pattern — we think our traffic was normal for the day, maybe a software-side rerun created a burst.
[01:20] Maya Singh: It looked like a replay from a job in the ingest pipeline; that created a non-uniform sequence length distribution which pushed memory usage. The runtime's continuous batching tried to pack, but batches became oversized and caused memory pressure, which then triggered cache eviction heuristics.
[01:55] Sophia Lane: So is this primarily a model serving config issue, or do we need infra changes?
[02:10] Jordan Patel: Short answer: both. There are tunables on the Redwood runtime (batch size caps, prefix cache retention) we can adjust immediately, and then infra-side we want to discuss an optional Dedicated fallback or isolated pool for high-priority tenants.
[02:35] Rachel Park: For us data residency & audit are also a requirement — any Dedicated talk needs to include KMS and SOC 2 compliance specifics.
[02:50] Liam Ortiz: Noted, Elysium already asked for the SOC 2 docs during the incident, we added that to the ticket.
[03:05] Maya Singh: On the cache itself: we recommend increasing per-tenant KV cache retention for Elysium by 20% and lowering max batch packing for long sequences to prevent oversizing. That should reduce eviction churn.
[03:35] Dmitri Ivanov: Any estimations on cost impact if we change those parameters? We have to balance latency and token costs.
[03:50] Jordan Patel: We'll run a quick bench test using your sample traffic; Maya will produce a cost delta. Expect a small per-token increase but reduced 5xx risk which is our bigger SLA worry.
[04:12] Rachel Park: The thing that worried us was the lack of obvious alerting before user-facing errors. We had metrics jump but the alert threshold was too conservative.
[04:30] Maya Singh: Agreed — add synthetic checks for key endpoints and token-level error rate alerts. We'll propose thresholds.
[05:00] Speaker 6: (brief crosstalk) sorry, just wanted to flag — the runtime logs named a module as Redwood-serve but transcript mangled it as 'read wood serve' in the auto transcript.
[05:20] Jordan Patel: (laughs) yes auto transcripts sometimes do that.
[05:40] Rachel Park: On the security side can you confirm audit logs persisted for the window? We need those for internal postmortem and for compliance.
[05:55] Maya Singh: Audit logs were persisted; we had a slight delay in upload for a single host but nothing lost. We'll attach the log pointers.
[06:20] Dmitri Ivanov: Walk me through the proposed Dedicated fallback. If we reserve a small dedicated pool with guaranteed KV cache, can we avoid this class of failure?
[06:38] Jordan Patel: The Dedicated pool gives isolated memory and CPU and predictable throughput. It also lets you pin model versions and control cache size per tenant. There is a cost/commit tradeoff, we'll provide numbers.
[06:58] Sophia Lane: Is there an intermediate option? Like reservation plus bursting?
[07:12] Maya Singh: Yes — reserved baseline capacity with on-demand burst. We can configure autoscale policies: keep a buffer of spare slots for Elysium during known high windows. That reduces cold starts and cache churn.
[07:40] Rachel Park: During the outage, some requests fell back to an older model variant with higher latency, which increased token counts. How do you prevent model fallback from happening silently?
[07:55] Jordan Patel: We have routing rules; we can tighten the fallback policy so model variant fallback only happens after X consecutive failures and with notification. Also add tracing so you can see which variant served each request.
[08:20] Dmitri Ivanov: On timelines — what can you deliver quickly?
[08:28] Maya Singh: Quick wins in 48-72 hours: change batch caps, tweak cache retention, add alerting. Medium-term (2-3 weeks): bench tests with your dataset, proposal for Dedicated fallback config, runbook changes. Long-term: consider per-tenant isolation options.
[08:50] Rachel Park: We need the runbook updates and a short implementation plan by 2025-10-20. Also want a meeting for the bench test results.
[09:05] Jordan Patel: We'll mark that as an action item.
[09:18] Sophia Lane: Any security gaps exposed? We heard mention of delayed audit log upload — is there a risk of tampering?
[09:30] Maya Singh: No tampering — uploads were queued; once connectivity restored they flushed. We use signed uploads and KMS-backed checksum. We'll include the S3/KMS pointer in the doc.
[09:50] Rachel Park: Ok. Also one request: include a sample of the token-level error traces so our engineering leads can correlate with app-side retry patterns.
[10:05] Maya Singh: We'll include token-level traces and a small script to parse them.
[10:25] Dmitri Ivanov: For cost modeling, is there a way to simulate the change?
[10:35] Jordan Patel: Yes, Maya will run bench tests with your representative payloads and show cost/latency tradeoffs. We'll include pre/post metrics.
[10:55] Speaker 2: (minor interruption) sorry, did you say we lost any user data?
[11:05] Maya Singh: No user data loss. Some requests errored but no persisted data was lost.
[11:20] Rachel Park: Good.
[11:30] Jordan Patel: Ok let's go through the action items again, and then open floor for any deep technical questions.
[11:40] Maya Singh: Action list: 1) runbook updates and draft autoscale policy, 2) KV cache param adjustments and bench tests, 3) token-trace export, 4) Dedicated pricing and config proposal, 5) alerting thresholds and synthetic checks.
[12:05] Dmitri Ivanov: For bench tests, can you replicate our exact sequence-length distribution? We can provide a sample trace.
[12:18] Maya Singh: Yes, please provide the sample trace and we'll run it through our harness. We may have to obfuscate PII but structure is fine.
[12:35] Rachel Park: We'll share it by 2025-10-18.
[12:45] Jordan Patel: Great. Final Q: do we need a formal follow-up postmortem doc? Or is this enough?
[12:58] Sophia Lane: Please produce a short postmortem doc with RCA, mitigation steps, and timeline — that will satisfy our compliance team.
[13:12] Jordan Patel: We'll draft that and circulate.
[13:25] Liam Ortiz: I'll set up the follow-up meeting for bench test review week of 2025-10-27, invitees to include Elysium SREs and Redwood SEs.
[13:40] Rachel Park: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[13:50] Jordan Patel: Thanks all — we'll send the notes and action items after this call.
[14:00] (meeting ends)
